items.title: I helped start OpenAI because I want AGI to be safe and beneficial for people. This post provides tr...
items.content:
I helped start OpenAI because I want AGI to be safe and beneficial for people. This post provides transparency that can be the foundation of industry-wide shared safety bars.

Perhaps the most important concept from the post is the following: "AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining."

Towards ensuring that safety keeps pace with general intelligence of pretrained models (as measured by "perplexity"), the post proposes "common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors)."

The general idea is to create a first shared limit, on some shared key metric, along with concrete exit criteria that would allow going beyond that. This can lead to a "common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development".

Excited to move forward the conversation on pacing towards shared standards that are rooted in the science!

items.content: @elonmusk @garrytan Honestly, deployment friction might actually be the best thing that could happen to the AI infra sector. It forces the AI buildout to get stretched over a much longer timeline. That keeps pricing power strong for the companies above, and it gives the applications side of AI enough breathing room to demonstrate commercial viability and catch up to the datacenter capex. Avoids having a big capacity spike followed by a glut.

items.title: "I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to e...
items.content:
"I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards.

I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors).

That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it."

- reading the internet (raw next-token pre-training)
- learning how to behave (supervised fine-tuning, RLHF)
- getting graded (RLVR)

He adds that mid-training, which he describes as pre-training on curated high-quality data, has emerged as a stage, though he believes the field can still improve on it.

@pabloestevezh @huxlab That risk is greatly overestimated. 
The information already exists and is available in textbooks.
Do you want to restrict who can study microbiology, infectious diseases, virology, etc?

AI systems merely make access to this information more efficient.
To produce new pathogens, you have to do experiments in the real-world.
It requires a team of well-trained PhDs. You will have to recruit them, kill them if the refuse to join, brainwash them so they work to kill millions (good luck with that), kill them if they defect, etc. 
Their PhD advisors will find their disappearance odd and will alert the authorities.
You'll have to order those machines that can synthesize DNA and such.
The whole R&D operation will be very hard to keep secret.
All the intelligence agencies will jump on you within weeks.

OpenAI proposes perplexity as the universal metric for industry self regulation and pacing (as opposed to eg FLOPS)

“Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window.”

this chart is one of the most beautiful ways to tell the story of the last 4 years. it also shows that a lot of the post training issues we debate is kinda the B plot to the overall A plot of large scale pretrain progress.

items.title: What did we just see with Riemann and what does it mean?  And why isn‘t it immediately rescuing the ...
items.content:
What did we just see with Riemann and what does it mean?  And why isn‘t it immediately rescuing the market?

A meditation on how many here are misunderstanding both the nature of and the implications of the Riemann results.

A key fact about the brilliant Riemann results that many people here are missing: AI *alone* did not solve the Reimann hypothesis. 

Instead an exceptionally talented mathematician with expertise in AI worked together with AI to jointly solve RH.  

As AI math pioneer @ChrSzegedy put, it “Levent made all the right (life) choices at the right time” in order to achieve the result, and we wouldn’t be here others. He didn’t just type in a prompt “Solve Riemann” and get the answer.

Fundamentally, rather, a brilliant mathematician with brilliant instanct drove the process. It took months and a lot of iteration.

And he relied on a special set of resources (see below) that you won’t did for example in medicine.

What actually happened is still super impressive — but it is not what thousands of people seem to believe, and it doesn’t have the same implications.

It does not mean for example that AGI has arrived, or anything like that. (If it had, you wouldn’t have needed the human mathematician to guide the whole process.) 

The other thing that a lot of people aren’t getting is that the RH solution depended on a special-purpose symbolic AI solver with 16 millions of lines of code - built over multiple years by perhaps hundreds  of people — for a specific purpose that is of relatively little value for solving more open-end problems in domains like biology, business, or robotics.  (As I predicted in 2024, verifiable methods have help more with math than other domains.)

Or as @jeremyakahn just put it “Solving RH doesn’t help you negotiate a contract better or correctly figure out a corporate tax return. So no real change to enterprise value prop.”  As @sebkrier put, “Solving an old pure math problem does not immediately widen Anthropic's operating margins"

It’s kind of like what we saw when DeepBlue beat @Kasparov63 in chess in 1997; an absolutely amazing use of brute force in a special-purpose way that didn’t generalize to all that much else. 

The market seems to get all of this - RH hasn’t moved $ANT much after hours – even if a lot of people here don’t.

Paraphrasing something I said here yesterday, clinging to the Riemann results like a life raft after the stock market correction doesn’t change the fact that (a) current AI still isn’t trustworthy enough to for many applications and (b) is still not profitable enough to warrant the massive investments.

items.title: @AdamCohen8 @haider1 As I pointed out multiple times to people like you who don't know better: mathe...
items.content:
@AdamCohen8 @haider1 As I pointed out multiple times to people like you who don't know better: mathematics (like code) is a special case where the correctness of a hypothesized object (proof, derivation, code) can be checked.
An AI system can therefore produce many objects, check their correctness (or estimate their quality), select the best, and adjust itself, until a proof (or a working code) is produced.
It is far from an auto-regressive LLM.
It performs inference by search, which is what I've been advocating for years.
But the search is performed in discrete token space, which works for math and code but not so well for everything else.
items.author: @ylecun
items.summary: LeCun explains that mathematics and code are special domains where correctness is verifiable, so AI can search over candidate proofs/programs and check them — inference by search in discrete token space — which he has long advocated, noting this approach does not extend well to other domains and is far from plain autoregressive LLMs.
items.reasoning: Substantive technical argument about search-based inference, verifiability, and architectural limitations from a leading researcher; moderate engagement but real intellectual content.

items.title:
Current systems can’t in fact solve biology.  The inductive argument below is flawed.

As I have bee...
items.content:
Current systems can’t in fact solve biology.  The inductive argument below is flawed.

As I have been saying here at least since 2024. there is a PRINCIPLED difference between math (which is quickly verifiable) and biology (which often takes lab work and can’t be verified in the same ways).

Importantly, different architectures have different capabilities and understanding that is key to making accurate predictions. Pure LLMs still can’t do math on their own; new, neurosymbolic architectures that integrate symbolic tools with LLMs etc can.  

Different types of systems have different capabilities, and you need to understand what a given class of systems can do to assess properly.

The final problem with the argument is below is that they muddle together things like pure LLMs with more complex systems that use LLMs as a larger component.  The scientific question was always about what an LLM could do its own; the argument i always made was that you should use them as a component in a  larger system, and that simple scaling alone wouldn’t be enough.  (That turned out to be correct.)

items.title: @john__allard Yes. The paper that popularized tool calls by LLMs, Toolformer, was published by my fo...
items.content:
@john__allard Yes. The paper that popularized tool calls by LLMs, Toolformer, was published by my former colleagues at FAIR in January 2023.
But my slides makes a specific statement that is correct: ***auto-regressive*** LLMs have a basic flaw.
You can fix it by making them no auto-regressive, e.g. by backtracking, search, tool use, multiple trial and error, etc.
One of the main points of my talks, and the main point of this slide, has been to advocate for inference/reasoning by ***search***, as opposed to auto-regressive prediction.

items.content_html:
@john__allard Yes. The paper that popularized tool calls by LLMs, Toolformer, was published by my former colleagues at FAIR in January 2023.

But my slides makes a specific statement that is correct: ***auto-regressive*** LLMs have a basic flaw.

You can fix it by making them no auto-regressive, e.g. by backtracking, search, tool use, multiple trial and error, etc.

One of the main points of my talks, and the main point of this slide, has been to advocate for inference/reasoning by ***search***, as opposed to auto-regressive prediction.

items.summary_html: LeCun quotes a long historical passage about the Ottoman Empire's delayed adoption of Arabic printing presses due to sultans' decrees, apparently as an analogy about technology adoption resistance.
items.content_html:
@rbzapp @huxlab "The establishment of the Arabic printing presses in the Ottoman Empire was delayed due to the fear of the sultans that some biased persons might tamper with the sacred religious texts. Hence, in 1485 Sultan Bayezid II (1447 or 8-1512) issued a royal decree prohibiting the use of printed books. A similar decree was issued in 1515 by the Sultan Selim I (1470-1520). However, these prohibitions were not applied to books printed by Dhimmis (or People of the Book, i.e. Christians and Jews). Hence, Presses for printing Hebrew books were founded at the end of the 15th century in Constantinople and other cities in the Ottoman Empire.

The first Arabic press to be established in the Ottoman Empire was founded in Constantinople, ca. 1720 during the reign of the Sultan Ahmed III (1673-1736) by the endeavors of Ahmet Efendi Celebi (أحمد أفندي چلبي) and his son Sait (سعيد) who enlisted the expertise of the Hungarian convert to Islam, the talented artisan and expert printer, İbrahim Muteferrika (إبراهيم متفرقة) (1674?-1745). The first Arabic book to be printed in this press was a translation into Ottoman Turkish of the Arabic lexicon al-Sihah (الصحاح) of al-Jawhari (d. 1003?) in the year 1728."

https://t.co/1Q46KKHyCb

items.title: ChapterPal goes offline. Its 2026 edition of the classic A Byte of Python by Swaroop C H is now avai...
items.content:
ChapterPal goes offline. Its 2026 edition of the classic A Byte of Python by Swaroop C H is now available on Amazon as a paperback and Kindle ebook.

Last month, I posted about my effort to restore classic computer science texts for ChapterPal's collection: https://t.co/9fgzvbG02X

Now this restored edition has a physical format, too.

I reworked about 30% of the original book's content and added several sections that I wrote for this edition and that describe features that weren't there when Swaroop wrote the book, like type hints or coding with AI.

Links to purchase A Byte of Python (2026) on Amazon: 

- US: https://t.co/awFyrTVjYc
- CA: https://t.co/n0RjyPv1k6
- DE: https://t.co/Kzb6j1bPvm
- UK: https://t.co/t3wdzsonGm

Soon, I'll publish a physical edition of another classic, Linux Fundamentals by Paul Cobbaut (2015), updated with 2026 distributions and tools.

Just arrived. Have 14 days to use them.

Now that I have them in my home instead of at a pre setup PR demo I can really put them through their paces and compare them to others. 

@getVITURE just sent me a new pair too. 

After using them I come away with one thing: augmented reality is so amazing.

I wish I could really show you how amazing it is. Been using them for an hour already and very different because you can still see the real reality through them better than on any of the others.

Which means they are truly augmenting reality.

It is fitting that I am wearing my @stevewoz shirt.

It is amazing how far we have come since my dad got an Apple II back in 1977 to where we can augment reality itself.

Now excuse me, I am having fun playing virtual ping pong against an AI.

I asked them to send me a pair so I could prepare for the Consumer Electronics Show coming in January.

These probably won’t go mainstream. Too expensive for me to afford, for one.

But devices like this are the future. Of that I am convinced.

And if you say “I will never wear glasses” well then you are missing out. Sucks to be you.

items.title: @MarcHoag @Nextdoor @TowneApp Here is what Grok learned by watching this video: https://t.co/wrLMA6B...
items.content:
@MarcHoag @Nextdoor @TowneApp Here is what Grok learned by watching this video: https://t.co/wrLMA6BBW6

**The ~42-minute video is a long-form conversation between tech commentator Robert Scoble and Marc Hoag, founder of TowneApp (also called Towne), an ad-free neighborhood social network positioned as an alternative to Nextdoor.**[](<https://t.co/pkWyAC8r4d>) Frames show Marc Hoag speaking outdoors (wearing a UCLA-patched vest) for much of the discussion, interspersed with Scoble in his studio setup. The content centers on Hoag’s motivation, the structural problems he sees in existing local platforms, Towne’s design choices, and his broader philosophy of community.[](<https://t.co/UwY8lxffY6>)

The founding story begins with Hoag’s direct experience on Nextdoor in October 2023. He posted a careful, polite essay in his Marin County (Mill Valley area) neighborhood arguing that opaque, top-down moderation undermines genuine community building. The post was deleted within about 50 minutes. He reposted it twice more; each version was also removed. Neighbors had engaged positively (likes and comments noting similar experiences with deleted posts), but the content disappeared. A separate informal poll he ran on the platform about how people access the app was also removed, labeled as spam without explanation. An informal snapshot of opinions among Marin Nextdoor users (cited around April 2026) showed very low satisfaction. This sequence crystallized the thesis that a neighborhood platform should strengthen connections rather than silence them, and it became the explicit founding document for Towne.[](<https://t.co/UwY8lxffY6>)

Hoag also draws on personal observation. During a two-year period in a small New England town (where his child was born), he saw families with sharply different political views living next to each other, disagreeing, teasing one another, and still maintaining real relationships. Local interactions felt more open. Returning to Marin, he noted a more constrained conversational climate. His wife (who grew up in communist Romania) observed cultural differences in how disagreement is handled. These experiences reinforced the goal of a space where different views can coexist without automatic removal or fear of deletion.[](<https://t.co/UwY8lxffY6>)

Towne’s design principles deliberately invert common social-network incentives. It is free, ad-free, and does not sell user data. Membership is neighbors-only and gated by a vouch from an existing neighbor (via single-use code), scoped primarily to ZIP codes, to keep the network real rather than open to strangers or growth-hacked contacts. Content ranking relies on community upvotes and downvotes rather than opaque engagement algorithms or a central moderation team. Political or highly civic posts are not deleted for viewpoint; neighbors can flag them separately from quality votes. Once a threshold is crossed, the post is moved (not hidden or penalized) into an opt-in “Towne Hall” channel dedicated to civic discussion, leaving the main feed cleaner. Harassment, threats, spam, and similar issues remain removable. Other features include channels for general discussion, recommendations (without star ratings or paid placements; businesses can claim free verified pages), events (with RSVP/calendar support), shared photos (up to four per post, with private controls), polls (anonymous voting), and planned or existing areas for safety alerts, marketplace, lost-and-found, and jobs/gigs. Early posters in a neighborhood can earn permanent “Founding Neighbor” badges. The service is available on the web and as a native iOS app (Swift/SwiftUI). Ranking and moderation use transparent rule-based systems rather than generative AI.[](<https://t.co/46G7B27PsD>)

Hoag’s background as a California-licensed attorney (since 2008), former founder of a VC-backed Series A jobs marketplace, host of a long-running autonomous-vehicles podcast, and fractional general counsel for AI/SaaS startups informed the build. He is a self-taught developer who constructed the product largely himself (web soft-launch around June 2026, iOS shortly after) through his company Axiomic, LLC, without external pressure to monetize attention. He has described the hardest product problem as handling politics without either deleting opinions or letting them dominate everyday neighborhood interaction. The approach prioritizes deliberate, neighborhood-by-neighborhood growth over rapid scaling tactics.[](<https://t.co/jmvNXWIuCs>)

In the conversation, the core argument is that local platforms fail when their business model or moderation incentives reward division, advertising, or centralized control rather than neighbor-to-neighbor utility. Towne aims to be “built by a neighbor, not a corporation,” with the explicit mission statement that people of different views and backgrounds should still form one community. The video presents this as a practical, experience-driven response to observed failures rather than a purely theoretical critique, with concrete product mechanisms (voting, political flagging + relocation, vouching, no ads) offered as the operational answer.[](<https://t.co/46G7B27PsD>)

Overall, the interview content frames TowneApp as an attempt to restore the practical utility and open character of neighborhood conversation while avoiding the structural incentives that have made existing platforms feel adversarial or heavily moderated for many users. The details above are drawn from the video’s context together with the primary materials Hoag and the project have published that align with what the discussion covers.

High Performance-Computing-The Likes of Which the World Had Never Seen Before!

items.content:
High Performance-Computing-The Likes of Which the World Had Never Seen Before! 

Back in 2015, with the publication of my pioneering research book, Big Data Appliances for In-Memory Computing, I was at the forefront of pioneering advances in high-performance computing, deep learning, machine learning, in-memory architectures, massively parallel processing, distributed systems, and machine learning—pushing the computational frontiers of scientific research and enterprise-grade intelligence. 

This was before NVIDIA introduced its DGX-1 deep-learning supercomputer in 2016, and long before GPU-accelerated AI became the defining force behind modern enterprise computing.

A pioneering exploration of computational performance, architectural innovation, and enterprise intelligence—more than a decade ahead of today's mainstream AI revolution! 

What do NASA's Pleiades supercomputer, SAP HANA, and Lockheed Martin's legendary SR-71 Blackbird have in common? 

Speed, agility, massively parallel engineering, and off-the-charts extraordinary computational high performance! 

NASA's Pleiades was an extraordinary example of distributed systems engineering. @NASA 

Unlike conventional shared-memory systems, Pleiades distributed computation across thousands of independent compute nodes, each maintaining its own physical memory.

Its sophisticated dual-plane InfiniBand interconnect, organized around a hypercube network topology, enabled high-bandwidth, low-latency communication between nodes.

How did the distributed architecture work?

Distributed Memory: Large scientific datasets and computational workloads were partitioned across independent nodes, avoiding dependence on a single machine's memory.

MPI Communication: Message Passing Interface enabled distributed processes to exchange data, C/C++, coordinate execution, and synchronize computational result.

GPU Acceleration: NVIDIA Tesla GPUs accelerated massively parallel numerical operations, including matrix computations essential to neural networks and scientific modeling.

GPU Computing: CPUs handled orchestration, data preparation, and general-purpose computation, while GPUs accelerated suitable high-throughput kernels.

Parallel Machine Learning: Independent data partitions could be processed concurrently, with synchronization or aggregation strategies determined by the algorithm.

Deep Belief Networks: NASA researchers employed hierarchical feature extraction and deep learning to classify high-resolution satellite imagery, demonstrating the convergence of GPU computing, machine learning, and large-scale scientific data processing.

The engineering challenge was not simply adding more processors. It was minimizing communication overhead,high performance optimization, balancing distributed workloads, optimizing memory locality, and maximizing computational throughput. 

'Tis the season.  Amazon poured the passion into the cover of the book with the copyright of Lockheed Martin’s world’s fastest jet-powered aircraft SR-71.  The next frontier in human evolution is big data, in-memory computing, and high-performance computing for building enterprise-grade analytics.  The book is for broader audience on how big data will shape the future of the industries.  Enjoy the book with your friends and family.  What is common between SAP HANA, SR-71 Blackbird, and Pleiades supercomputer? 

It is the speed, agility, and off-the-charts dynamic performance. More in the book. 

Some pages of the book have already appeared on my Facebook's timeline in the past few years.  The back of the cover is from one of my Facebook’s single post.  Thank you very much for your staunch support over an extended arc of time.  All of you, please give a thumbs-up for the book.  Write a sentence or two on Amazon or on Goodreads when it is out in the first week of December, 2015.  I will post more links once it is available. The book will be available in Paperback (Americas and Europe) or Global Kindle Editions of your preference.  If you need an autographed book, please let me know.

High Performance-Computing-The Likes of Which the World Had Never Seen Before!

Back in 2015, with the publication of my pioneering research book, Big Data Appliances for In-Memory Computing, I was at the forefront of pioneering advances in high-performance computing, deep learning, machine learning, in-memory architectures, massively parallel processing, distributed systems, and machine learning—pushing the computational frontiers of scientific research and enterprise-grade intelligence.

This was before NVIDIA introduced its DGX-1 deep-learning supercomputer in 2016, and long before GPU-accelerated AI became the defining force behind modern enterprise computing.

A pioneering exploration of computational performance, architectural innovation, and enterprise intelligence—more than a decade ahead of today's mainstream AI revolution!

What do NASA's Pleiades supercomputer, SAP HANA, and Lockheed Martin's legendary SR-71 Blackbird have in common?

Speed, agility, massively parallel engineering, and off-the-charts extraordinary computational high performance!

NASA's Pleiades was an extraordinary example of distributed systems engineering. @NASA

Unlike conventional shared-memory systems, Pleiades distributed computation across thousands of independent compute nodes, each maintaining its own physical memory.

Its sophisticated dual-plane InfiniBand interconnect, organized around a hypercube network topology, enabled high-bandwidth, low-latency communication between nodes.

How did the distributed architecture work?

Distributed Memory: Large scientific datasets and computational workloads were partitioned across independent nodes, avoiding dependence on a single machine's memory.

MPI Communication: Message Passing Interface enabled distributed processes to exchange data, C/C++, coordinate execution, and synchronize computational result.

GPU Acceleration: NVIDIA Tesla GPUs accelerated massively parallel numerical operations, including matrix computations essential to neural networks and scientific modeling.

GPU Computing: CPUs handled orchestration, data preparation, and general-purpose computation, while GPUs accelerated suitable high-throughput kernels.

Parallel Machine Learning: Independent data partitions could be processed concurrently, with synchronization or aggregation strategies determined by the algorithm.

Deep Belief Networks: NASA researchers employed hierarchical feature extraction and deep learning to classify high-resolution satellite imagery, demonstrating the convergence of GPU computing, machine learning, and large-scale scientific data processing.

The engineering challenge was not simply adding more processors. It was minimizing communication overhead,high performance optimization, balancing distributed workloads, optimizing memory locality, and maximizing computational throughput.

'Tis the season. Amazon poured the passion into the cover of the book with the copyright of Lockheed Martin’s world’s fastest jet-powered aircraft SR-71. The next frontier in human evolution is big data, in-memory computing, and high-performance computing for building enterprise-grade analytics. The book is for broader audience on how big data will shape the future of the industries. Enjoy the book with your friends and family. What is common between SAP HANA, SR-71 Blackbird, and Pleiades supercomputer?

It is the speed, agility, and off-the-charts dynamic performance. More in the book.

Some pages of the book have already appeared on my Facebook's timeline in the past few years. The back of the cover is from one of my Facebook’s single post. Thank you very much for your staunch support over an extended arc of time. All of you, please give a thumbs-up for the book. Write a sentence or two on Amazon or on Goodreads when it is out in the first week of December, 2015. I will post more links once it is available. The book will be available in Paperback (Americas and Europe) or Global Kindle Editions of your preference. If you need an autographed book, please let me know.

items.title: Research indicates that Asians often experience the onset of visible wrinkles and crow’s feet in the...
items.content:
Research indicates that Asians often experience the onset of visible wrinkles and crow’s feet in their late 30s to early 40s. This delay is largely attributed to the naturally higher collagen content found in Asian skin. However, individual factors such as genetics and sun exposure and how much they laugh can influence this timeline significantly. In fact, some studies highlight that certain Asian individuals may notice the first signs wrinkles, smile line, dark circles and crowfeet of aging as early as their early 30s. Understanding these variations can help in taking proactive measures for skin care.  Yang et al. found that wrinkle measures increased more noticeably at ages 31–42 and changed more rapidly.  The authors did report seeing crow’s feet as early as about 23 at the outer corner of the eyes apart from lines under the eyes.

items.content:
I love Billie Eilish. I believe that she is the only artist of the past two decades who could invent a new style of music that many modern young artists have now adopted.

And I totally support her ostentatious disregard for style and for conforming to society's imposed notions of how a female artist should look. She's rich and talented. Fuck the style.

But where did she get my Turkish shirt and my glasses from when I was a student in Ukraine in 1999?

(The awesome song: https://t.co/tSDobAsGDu)
